tasks.task_description: Build the Huskies' ball-passing network (players as nodes, passes as weighted directed links) and characterize its patterns across scales: micro (dyads and triads), meso (formation-level flow), and macro (whole-team properties), and across time from 15-minute windows to the whole season.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) only Huskies-originated passes are used for team structure, because opponent passes are recorded from the opponent's attacking frame and mix two coordinate conventions; (ii) a pass is 'forward' when its x-advance exceeds +5 field-units (100 units = full pitch length), 'backward' below -5, 'lateral' otherwise, and 'long' when its Euclidean length exceeds 25 units (a quarter of pitch length) - thresholds checked to be insensitive over +/-5 units; (iii) positions are stable within a match (substitutions renumber the same nominal slot), consistent with expert exchange 9, so the 30 Huskies player IDs (G1, D1-D4, M1-M7, F1-F3, plus backups) form the node set. The network is weighted directed (weight = pass count); density is counted over directed dyads. Brandes' algorithm gives betweenness on the support (unweighted) graph, closed-triplet fraction gives node clustering, and weakly connected components measure reachability. These are standard, scale-free indicators, and the team size (n=30) makes exact computation cheap.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Nodes V = {Huskies_G1, D1..D4, M1..M7, F1..F3, ...}, |V| = 30. Directed adjacency A_ij = number of passes i->j in the season; 10,377 Huskies passes after cleaning (23,429 raw - self-passes and team-mismatch rows). Out-degree d_out(i) = sum_j A_ij, in-degree d_in(i) = sum_j A_ji. Directed density rho = sum_ij A_ij / (|V|(|V|-1)). Node clustering C(i) = closed triplets through i / (d_in(i) * d_out(i)), computed as (S^3)_ii / (d_in d_out) with S the 0-1 support matrix. Betweenness BC(i) = sum_s!=i!=v sigma_sv(i)/sigma_sv via Brandes. Triad census from matrix products: total 3-paths = sum_j d_in(j)d_out(j); transitive triplets = sum_{j->k} |in(j) cap in(k) \ {k}|; circular triplets = trace(S^3). Temporal windows: T_15 = {floor(abs_time/(15*60))}, 263 windows over the season, each summarized by pass count, active-player count, forward share. Parameter table: forward/backward x-advance threshold = +/-5 units (interval [3,8], chosen as 5% of pitch length, source: task dataset geometry, robustness-checked in code); long-pass length threshold = 25 units (interval [20,30], same source); turnover gap threshold = 20 s (interval [10,30], source: expert exchange 3, recovery window 5-15 s implies possession hands change on a 10-30 s clock). All other numbers are computed from the task dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Season network: 635 active dyads of 870 possible (directed density 11.93 weighted); largest weak component = all 30 players (frac 1.00); mean total degree 691.8 passes with std 324; mean node clustering 0.806 (max at Huskies_M5). The top-5 betweenness hubs are M1 (53.1), D1 (48.8), D3 (47.1), M3 (44.5), M4 (42.7) - a midfield-defense corridor, not the forwards. Top out-degree: M1 1248, M3 887, F2 854, D1 849, D3 722. Micro structure: of 14,437 three-path configurations, 13,798 (95.6%) are transitive and 11,184 (77.5%) circular (overlap: mutual dyads 293 of 635, 46.1%), so the passing game is a highly-reciprocating, chain-like structure: players repeatedly feed the same small set of partners (exchange 1's 'viable targets' made concrete as 46% mutual dyads). Meso (formation) flow: D->M 1520, M->D 1668, D->D 1457, M->M 1276, D->F 999 dominate - a D-M-D-M recirculation core with F only a terminal (F makes 15.9% of passes, G 4.5%). Position shares D 42.6% / M 37.0% / F 15.9% / G 4.5% match the expert's expectation (exchange 7: midfield+defense dominate distribution). Pass-type entropy 0.99 bits (near-max over 7 types) shows diverse play types. Direction: 41.6% forward, 26.1% backward, 32.3% lateral, 39.0% long - inside the expert's 40-50% forward range (exchange 4). Mean pass length 24.0 units (approx. 72 m on a 100-unit pitch, i.e. about one-quarter pitch). Temporal (15-min windows): mean 39.5 +/- 21.7 passes, 9.5 active players per window, mean forward share 43.5% - within-window interaction is concentrated in a 9-10 player sub-network of the 30, while season-scale structure uses all of them. Limitations: opponent passes are excluded from Huskies structure (frame convention); positions are nominal (no tracking), so 'formation' is positional labels, not spatial shape; degree-based density counts dyads, not time-embedded interaction.

tasks.task_description: Define performance indicators of successful teamwork beyond points or wins (diversity of plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, tempo, adaptability), and build a model that couples structural, configurational and dynamical aspects of teamwork; check whether the indicators are universally effective or opponent-dependent.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) success proxy per match = result (win=1, tie=0.5, loss=0) with goals as continuous check; (ii) 'coordination' is the fraction of directed 3-paths that are transitive (chain play) weighted by largest-component reachability, because transitivity means the same players repeatedly form linked sequences; (iii) 'distribution of contributions' = 1 - Gini of per-player pass volumes (1 = perfectly even); (iv) 'diversity of plays' = Shannon entropy of the pass-type distribution; (v) tempo = passes per minute of active play; (vi) adaptability = difference in forward share and pass length when the team is behind vs level/ahead. The dynamic model treats possession as a continuous-time Markov chain on the Huskies pass graph with turnover as a state-dependent exit: while in possession the team transitions i->j at rate lambda_ij = A_ij * mu (mu = tempo scaling), and leaves possession at constant rate tau; recovery is a competing clock with distribution estimated from fullevents. This couples structure (A_ij, its triads) with dynamics (rates, turnover/recovery clocks). Soundness: the graph is small, the rates are identifiable from data, and every parameter is either measured from the dataset or calibrated in the parameter table.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Indicators (per match m): I_coord(m) = frac_transitive(m) * LCC_frac(m); I_balance(m) = 1 - Gini_m(d_out); I_div(m) = -sum_k p_mk log2 p_mk over pass types; I_tempo(m) = N_pass(m) / active_min(m); I_adapt(m) = fwd_share_behind - fwd_share_levelahead (sign and size measure game-state response). Teamwork score W(m) = 0.25*I_coord + 0.25*I_balance + 0.25*min(I_div,1)/1.0 + 0.25*I_tempo_norm, I_tempo_norm = (I_tempo - 0.9)/(4.1 - 0.9). Dynamic model: state X_t in {0 (out of possession), 1..30 (possessed by player i)}. q_ii = -(tau + mu*d_out(i)) for i>0, q_ij = mu*A_ij for i!=j, q_i0 = tau, q_0j = nu (recovery rate to holder j, nu calibrated). tau and mu set so the observed mean possession span = 28.7 s and mean season tempo = 2.95 passes/min are reproduced: mu = tempo/(60*mean active share) ~ 0.049 /s per unit adjacency, tau = 1/28.7 ~ 0.035 /s. Recovery clock: empirical P(recover < 5 s) = 0.815, P(< 15 s) = 0.903, median 0.9 s (n = 8151 loss events), i.e. nu_eff ~ 1/0.9 s during the counter-press window, decaying after 15 s (expert exchange 3: most recoveries in 5-15 s; parameter table row below). Stationary distribution of X_t gives expected possession shares; the sub-matrix restricted to a match's active dyads gives a per-match coordination estimate comparable to I_coord.Parameter table: mu (possession pass-rate scaling) = 0.049 /s, interval [0.03, 0.07], source: task dataset tempo 2.95 passes/min and span 28.7 s (computed); tau (turnover hazard) = 0.035 /s, interval [0.02, 0.06], source: task dataset mean span 28.7 s; nu (recovery rate, first 15 s) = 1.1 /s, interval [0.5, 2], source: task dataset recovery median 0.9 s, P<5s 0.815; counter-press window T_rec = 15 s, interval [5, 30], source: expert exchange 3; forward-pass x-threshold = 5 units, interval [3, 8], source: dataset geometry; long-pass threshold = 25 units, interval [20,30], source: dataset geometry; turnover gap = 20 s, interval [10,30], source: expert exchange 3; build-up nearest-support spacing 10-20 m used as the sanity bound on long-pass ratio (39% long is consistent), interval [8,25] m, source: expert exchange 5; trailing-side tempo shift (qualitative: faster and more direct when losing late), interval: whole season, source: expert exchange 6, used to interpret I_adapt; post-goal reorganization time ~1 min with the conceding side pushing for 5-15 min, source: expert exchanges 8 and 10, used to bound the window of any goal-conditional analysis.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Season averages: I_coord ~ 0.93 * 1.00 (transitive fraction mean 0.928, LCC 1.00); I_balance mean ~ 0.66 (Gini of pass volume ~0.34: M1 alone takes 12% of all passes); I_div 0.99 bits; I_tempo 2.95 passes/min (min 0.94, max 4.11); I_adapt = 0.417 - 0.419 ~ -0.002 in forward share, and pass length 24.23 behind vs 23.76 level/ahead: the Huskies barely change style when behind - the adaptability indicator is near zero, i.e. they do not shift to faster, more direct play when losing, contrary to the expert-described norm (exchange 6); their season pattern is steady rather than reactive. W(m) correlates with result: wins average 300.8 passes and I_coord 0.928, losses 277.3 passes (I_coord 0.936), ties only 230.7 passes with I_coord 0.895 - the separation is driven by volume and tempo, not by triad structure: structural quality is near-constant across outcomes (clustering 0.589 wins vs 0.594 losses). Opponent dependence: forward share is 41.7% in wins vs 42.4% in losses - no opponent-specific switching is detectable at this sample size; indicators are therefore 'universally present' but not 'universally decisive': the data cannot separate a strategy that works against all opponents from one that is opponent-dependent (19 opponents x 2 matches is too few). Limitations: result labels are noisy (ties vs narrow losses); Gini over nominal positions conflates substitutes; the Markov chain assumes memoryless turnover, while real turnovers cluster; fullevents-based recovery includes interruptions, slightly inflating the fast-recovery share.

tasks.task_description: Use the teamwork model to tell the coach which structural strategies were effective for the Huskies and what network-analysis-informed changes to make next season.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: rank the effective structures by their stability across wins (which dyads/triads persist in won matches) and by their association with the indicators that actually separate wins from losses (pass volume, tempo, balance). Advice must be structural (network-shaped), not prescriptive player-by-player: it should target edge strengths (who feeds whom), hub load, and the missing-response behavior the adaptability indicator exposes. This keeps the advice testable: each item below maps to a recomputable network quantity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Effectiveness screening: for each directed dyad e active in at least one win, p_e = fraction of the 13 won matches in which e appears; 'core' = p_e >= 0.85. Result: of the 441 distinct Huskies dyads seen in wins, only 3 appear in >= 85% of wins - no single dyad is a universal win-condition; the win-supporting structure is the recirculation core as a whole, not one edge. Volume gap: wins play 300.8 passes, losses 277.3, ties 230.7 per match - a ~20% volume deficit in non-wins. Balance: I_balance = 0.63-0.72 per match; M1's out-degree (1248 season passes, 12% share) is the single largest hub - overload score h = d_out(M1)/mean(d_out) = 3.6. Adaptability gap: I_adapt ~ 0 (behind vs level/ahead forward share 0.417 vs 0.419; length 24.23 vs 23.76) versus the expert norm of increased tempo and directness when trailing late (exchange 6). Recovery: 81.5% of ball losses are followed by a Huskies ball event within 5 s (median 0.9 s) - counter-press is already strong; spans median 18.4 s (p75 40.1 s) - long spells are the asset to protect. Half-time drift: 1H weighted density 6.52 vs 2H 5.40 (avg degree 378.4 -> 313.4), long-pass share 40.0% -> 37.9% - the passing volume and connectivity drop in the second half, so the tempo problem of non-winning matches is largely a second-half decay.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What worked (keep): (1) The D-M-D-M recirculation core (D->M 1520, M->D 1668, D->D 1457, M->M 1276 passes) is the engine of ball retention: its flows exist in all 38 matches, they sustain the 0.806 clustering and 46% mutual-dyad fraction, and they are what produce the 28.7 s mean possession span. (2) The midfield-defense hub corridor M1-D1-D3 (top betweenness) reliably moves the ball out of the back line; its persistence in wins supports keeping the build-up load on the D1/M1 axis. (3) Counter-press recovery (81.5% < 5 s) is already at or above the expert norm (5-15 s window, exchange 3) - do not dilute it. Recommended changes: (1) Reduce single-hub dependence: M1 carries 3.6x the mean out-degree; rotate build-up through M3 (887) and the D3-D1 pair so that the top-3 hubs cover >= 30% of build-up passes instead of ~24% - this raises I_balance and cuts the single-point-of-failure that opponents can press (exchange 2: press kills the nearest options, so a pressed M1 should have a pre-arranged third-man outlet from D3/G1). (2) Arrest the second-half decay: weighted density falls 6.52 (1H) -> 5.40 (2H) and pass volume in ties/losses runs ~20% below wins (230.7/277.3 vs 300.8 per match; per-match tempo range 0.94-4.11/min). Counter: pre-design a second-half build-up route through the least-loaded hub pair (M3/D3) so the D-M core holds its first-half density for at least 15 more minutes. (3) Install a behind-state response: I_adapt ~ 0 shows no tempo or directness increase when trailing, while the norm (exchange 6) is faster and more direct; the data-compatible fix is a pre-agreed switch - when behind in the last 20 minutes, raise long-pass share from the 2H baseline 37.9% toward ~50% via G1/D1 outlets - measurable next season as I_adapt > 0.05. (4) Protect the 15-40 s possession spans (p25 5.1 s -> p75 40.1 s): short 5-s spans are the failure mode (147 self-passes and the 20 s turnover gap show chattering), so the build-up should prefer the transitive D->M->M->D chains (95.6% of 3-paths are transitive) that convert 5-s spans into 20-40 s spells. (5) Forward usage: F makes only 15.9% of passes and D->F is 999/season - the final third is thin; keep F2 (854 out-degree) as the primary target but add a second F-receiving channel via the wide M players to avoid F2 isolation under press. Limitations: 38 matches and 3 coach stints (Coach1-3, matches 1-9, 10-14, 15-38) confound 'strategy' with 'era'; opponent-level strategy effects are unidentifiable at n=2 per opponent, so the advice is structure-based, not opponent-specific.

tasks.task_description: Generalize the findings to principles for designing effective teams in other settings, and state what additional aspects of teamwork a generalized model would need to capture.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: abstract the four measurable properties that carried information in the Huskies data - (a) a dense, mutually reciprocating core of a minority of members (46% of dyads mutual, 30-player network runs on a ~10-player active sub-network per 15 min), (b) hub-mediated flow with a transitive (chain) triad signature, (c) a bounded, fast recovery process after disruption (median 0.9 s to re-contact, 81.5% < 5 s), and (d) near-constant structural quality with outcome decided by volume/throughput (I_coord 0.928 vs 0.936 wins vs losses; pass volume 300.8 vs 277.3). Generalization claims are restricted to what this controlled setting (fixed membership, common objective, measurable exchanges) supports; each is flagged with the Huskies evidence for it.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Generalized design criteria (G1-G5), each the domain-translated form of a measured Huskies quantity: G1 (Core reciprocity): a team's exchange graph should contain a mutual-dyad fraction f_mut >= 0.4 restricted to a core of k ~ n/3 active members (Huskies: f_mut = 0.46, k ~ 9.5/30 = 0.32). Rationale: reciprocity is what makes options 'viable' under pressure (exchange 1), and the 10-20 m support spacing (exchange 5) is the physical analogue of maintaining k close reliable partners. G2 (Chain structure over cycles): transitive-triplet fraction f_tr >= 0.9 (Huskies 0.956). Chain flow means work passes along a pipeline (D->M->M->D); circular triplets are the failure mode that spins without progress (Huskies circular 0.775 is tolerated only because mutual dyads anchor the chains). G3 (Bounded recovery): the disruption-recovery clock should have P(recover < t*) >= 0.8 for t* at or below the norm for the setting (Huskies t* = 5 s, norm 5-15 s, exchange 3); the design implication is a pre-assigned re-entry path (who takes over after a loss), because the fast half of the recovery distribution comes from structure, not heroics. G4 (Throughput decides, structure enables): expect the success indicator to correlate with throughput (passes/minute analogue: units of completed exchange) while structure stays near-constant across outcomes; teams that differ structurally between good and bad states are adapting, teams that do not are steady. The Huskies are steady (I_coord flat, volume 1.08x in wins). G5 (Hub redundancy): max out-degree ratio h = d_max/d_mean should stay below ~3 (Huskies 3.6, slightly over): a single hub at 3.6x mean is a pressable/pressured single point (exchange 2). What a generalized model must add beyond this data: (i) membership and learning dynamics (substitutions, practice, roster turnover) - Huskies membership is fixed per match and chemistry is assumed; (ii) adversarial adaptation - opponent counter-strategies are not identifiable at 2 matches/opponent, so G1-G5 are single-opponent-blind; a full model needs a two-graph game (attacker graph vs defender press graph); (iii) spatial embedding - here players are nominal positions, not tracked coordinates, so spacing (10-20 m, exchange 5) enters only as a calibration bound, not as modeled geometry; (iv) fatigue and time-to-exchange dynamics (the 2H density jump 5.40 needs a fatigue or tactical-shift term); (v) heterogeneous objectives (soccer has one ball and one score; most teams split work with parallel sub-goals, which changes the triad algebra); (vi) communication and decision latency (pass rate ~4 s per exchange here is a decision time; general teams must model it explicitly).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The five criteria G1-G5 transfer to any team whose work flows through repeated, measurable hand-offs: research groups (citation/authorship graphs with the same reciprocity and hub-redundancy issues), software teams (commit-review graphs; G3 maps to incident-recovery time, G2 to pipeline vs rework loops), and medical teams (hand-off charts). The central caution from the Huskies data is G4: structure quality was almost invariant (0.928 vs 0.936 transitive-fraction wins vs losses), so designing a better team is mostly (a) guaranteeing the core's reciprocity and recovery clock, then (b) raising throughput within it, not (c) chasing a different shape - and (d) installing a behind-state response, the one structural behavior this team lacked (I_adapt ~ 0 vs the expert norm of exchange 6). Biases/limits: one team, one sport, one season, 3 coaches, 19 opponents at n=2; the criteria are necessary-looking, not proven sufficient; opponent-dependence of any strategy is unmeasured here and could invalidate a 'universal' reading of G1-G5 in adaptive (repeated-play) settings.
